html:
The Sixteen Kingdoms were the many short-lived states that ruled northern China from 304 to 439. The map shows them in 400.

They grew out of the collapse of the Jin dynasty. Non-Chinese peoples who had settled inside the frontier, the "Five Barbarians", rose up: the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Jie and Qiang. Xiongnu forces sacked Luoyang in 311 and Chang'an in 316. The Jin court fled south and ruled from Jiankang, now Nanjing, as the Eastern Jin.

In the north, states with Chinese-style names such as Former Zhao, Later Zhao, Former Yan and Later Qin rose and fell, usually within a few decades. One came close to reuniting China: the Former Qin unified the north by 376, but its huge army was beaten by the Eastern Jin at the Fei River in 383, and it broke apart.

The chaos helped Buddhism spread. The monk Kumarajiva translated scriptures at Chang'an for the Later Qin. The period ended in 439, when the Xianbei Northern Wei united the north.
sum: The Sixteen Kingdoms were the many short-lived states that ruled northern China from 304 to 439. The map shows them in 400.
